name: cs101_eval
description: 40 CS-101 tutor prompts with reference answers: 16 easy, 12 medium, 12 hard. Includes 4 paraphrase pairs (items 1/2, 5/6, 9/10, 13/14) to exercise the semantic cache.

items.prompt: what is a variable in python
items.reference: A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory, created by assignment (x = 5). Python variables are dynamically typed: the same name can later refer to a value of another type.

items.prompt: explain variables in python like im new to coding
items.reference: A variable is a labelled box/name for a value, created with = (age = 18). You can read it later, reassign it, and Python figures out the type from the value.

items.prompt: how do i write a comment in python
items.reference: Use # for a single-line comment; everything after # on that line is ignored. Multi-line notes are usually several # lines (triple-quoted strings are docstrings, not true comments).

items.prompt: what does len() do in python
items.reference: len(x) returns the number of items in a sequence or collection: characters in a string, elements in a list/tuple, keys in a dict, items in a set. e.g. len('abc') == 3.

items.prompt: what is a list in python
items.reference: An ordered, mutable collection written with square brackets, e.g. [1, 'a', 3.0]. Supports indexing from 0, slicing, append/remove, and can hold mixed types.

items.prompt: python lists what are they
items.reference: An ordered, mutable collection written with square brackets, e.g. [1, 'a', 3.0]. Supports indexing from 0, slicing, append/remove, and can hold mixed types.

items.prompt: what is the difference between a list and a tuple
items.reference: Lists are mutable ([ ]) — you can change, add, remove items. Tuples are immutable (( )) — fixed after creation, hashable (can be dict keys if contents are hashable), slightly faster, used for fixed records.

items.prompt: what does == vs === do in javascript
items.reference: == compares after type coercion ('5' == 5 is true); === compares value AND type without coercion ('5' === 5 is false). Prefer ===.

items.prompt: what is a hash map
items.reference: A data structure storing key→value pairs. A hash function maps each key to a bucket index so lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average; collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing. Python's dict is one.

items.prompt: explain hashmaps to me like im dumb
items.reference: Like a coat check: you hand over a key (ticket), a hash function turns it into a slot number, and the value is stored there, so finding it later is instant (O(1) average). Python's dict is a hash map.

items.prompt: what is a boolean
items.reference: A data type with only two values, True or False (true/false in JS). Produced by comparisons (3 > 2) and used in if/while conditions and logical operators and/or/not.

items.prompt: what is an infinite loop
items.reference: A loop whose condition never becomes false (or has no exit), e.g. while True: without break, or forgetting to update the loop variable. The program runs forever until stopped.

items.prompt: difference between print and return in python
items.reference: print() displays a value on the screen and gives back None; return sends a value back to the caller of a function so it can be stored or used, and ends the function. A function that only prints returns None.

items.prompt: what is recursion
items.reference: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, with a base case that stops the recursion. e.g. factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1), factorial(0) = 1. Without a base case you get infinite recursion / RecursionError.

items.prompt: wait so a function calls itself?? how does that even work
items.reference: Yes — each call gets its own frame on the call stack with its own variables. It keeps calling with a smaller input until a base case returns directly, then the results return back up the stack. e.g. factorial.

items.prompt: what is an f-string in python
items.reference: A string literal prefixed with f that evaluates expressions inside {}: f'Hello {name}, you are {age+1}'. Supports format specs like {x:.2f}. Python 3.6+.

items.prompt: how do i reverse a string in python
items.reference: s[::-1] using slicing with step -1. Alternatives: ''.join(reversed(s)). Strings are immutable, so this creates a new string.

items.prompt: write a python function that checks if a number is prime
items.reference: Return False for n < 2; check divisors from 2 up to int(n**0.5) inclusive; if any divides n return False, else True. O(sqrt(n)).

items.prompt: how do i read a text file line by line in python
items.reference:
with open('file.txt') as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip('\n'))
The with statement closes the file automatically; iterating the file object reads lazily line by line.

items.prompt: what is big o notation, give examples
items.reference: Describes how running time/space grows with input size n, ignoring constants. Examples: O(1) dict lookup, O(log n) binary search, O(n) loop over a list, O(n log n) sorting, O(n^2) nested loops over the same list.

items.prompt: when should i use a loop vs recursion
items.reference: Use loops for simple linear repetition (more memory-efficient; Python has a recursion limit ~1000 and no tail-call optimisation). Use recursion for naturally recursive structures: trees, nested data, divide-and-conquer (merge sort), backtracking.

items.prompt: how do try and except work in python
items.reference: Code in try runs; if an exception occurs, the matching except block handles it instead of crashing. Catch specific exceptions (except ValueError:), optionally else (runs if no exception) and finally (always runs, e.g. cleanup).

items.prompt: what is the difference between a class and an object
items.reference: A class is a blueprint/template defining attributes and methods; an object (instance) is a concrete thing created from it with its own data. e.g. class Dog: ... ; d = Dog('Rex') — Dog is the class, d is an object.

items.prompt: how do i count how many times each word appears in a sentence in python
items.reference: Split the string and count with a dict or collections.Counter: from collections import Counter; Counter(sentence.lower().split()). Optionally strip punctuation first.

items.prompt: explain list comprehensions with an example
items.reference: A concise way to build a list from an iterable: [expr for x in iterable if condition]. e.g. squares of evens: [x*x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0] → [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]. Equivalent to a for loop with append.

items.prompt: what is the difference between let, const and var in javascript
items.reference: var is function-scoped and hoisted (initialised as undefined) and can be redeclared. let and const are block-scoped, in a temporal dead zone before declaration; let can be reassigned, const cannot be reassigned (but objects it points to can still be mutated). Prefer const, then let.

items.prompt: how does binary search work
items.reference: On a sorted array, compare the target to the middle element; if equal, done; if smaller, search the left half, else the right half; repeat until found or the range is empty. O(log n). Requires sorted input.

items.prompt: what does the self keyword mean in python classes
items.reference: self is the first parameter of instance methods and refers to the specific object the method was called on; it is used to access/set that object's attributes (self.name = name). Python passes it automatically: d.bark() is Dog.bark(d).

items.prompt:
my python code gives 'IndexError: list index out of range' here:
```python
nums = [3, 1, 4]
for i in range(len(nums) + 1):
    print(nums[i])
```
why and how do i fix it
items.reference: range(len(nums)+1) produces 0..3 but valid indices are 0..2, so nums[3] fails. Use range(len(nums)), or better iterate directly: for n in nums: print(n).

items.prompt:
debug this, it always prints the same thing:
```python
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add_item(1))
print(add_item(2))
```
expected [1] then [2]
items.reference: Mutable default argument: the default list is created once at function definition and shared across calls, so the second call prints [1, 2]. Fix: def add_item(item, items=None): if items is None: items = [].

items.prompt: implement a stack class in python with push, pop, peek and is_empty, and explain the time complexity of each
items.reference: Use a list internally: push = append, pop = list.pop() (raise/handle on empty), peek = items[-1], is_empty = len(items) == 0. All are O(1) (append amortised O(1)).

items.prompt: write merge sort in python and explain how it works step by step
items.reference: Recursively split the list in halves until size ≤ 1, then merge two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element. Correct code with a merge helper. O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space, stable.

useEffect has no dependency array, so it runs after every render; setItems triggers a new render → infinite fetch/render loop. Fix: add [cat] as the dependency array (optionally handle cleanup/abort for stale requests).

items.prompt: explain the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy in python with an example where it matters
items.reference: A shallow copy (list.copy(), copy.copy, a[:]) copies the outer container but shares nested objects; a deep copy (copy.deepcopy) recursively copies everything. Example: a=[[1],[2]]; b=a.copy(); b[0].append(9) also changes a[0]; with deepcopy it does not.

items.prompt: design a simple class structure for a library system with books, members and loans. show python code and explain your design choices
items.reference: Classes Book (isbn, title, author, available), Member (id, name, loans), Loan (book, member, due date, returned), and a Library that manages checkout/return enforcing availability and limits. Explain separation of responsibilities, composition, validation.

refactor this to be more pythonic and explain each change:
```python
result = []
for i in range(len(names)):
    if names[i] != '':
        result.append(names[i].upper())
```
items.reference: result = [name.upper() for name in names if name] — iterate items directly instead of indices, use truthiness for the empty check, use a list comprehension instead of append loop.
O(n^2) because of the nested loops. Faster O(n) using a set: track seen values and return True on repeat, or return len(set(nums)) != len(nums). Trade-off: O(n) extra memory.

items.prompt: explain how python's dictionary handles collisions and why lookups are still O(1) on average
items.reference: Keys are hashed to a slot index; CPython uses open addressing with a perturbation-based probe sequence on collision. The table is resized (kept below ~2/3 full) so probe sequences stay short, giving O(1) average lookups; worst case O(n) with many collisions.

items.prompt: write a python function to find the most frequent element in a list, handle ties by returning the smallest one, and write 3 test cases
items.reference: Count with Counter or a dict, find max count, return min of elements with that count; handle empty list (return None or raise). Three asserts covering a normal case, a tie (smallest returned), and a single-element or empty case.

items.prompt: why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 return False in python and how should i compare floats
items.reference: Floats are binary (IEEE 754) and 0.1/0.2 cannot be represented exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance: math.isclose(a, b) or abs(a-b) < 1e-9; use decimal.Decimal or fractions for exact decimal arithmetic.
